Case Studies
Two case studies were developed based on the exploratory analysis conducted by an art
historian using the ArtVis Embedding Explorer. The first case study investigates how artists
associated with the Munich Secession are distributed across the embedding and shows how
the system can reveal an unusual form of participation. The second case study examines the
relationship between Alexej von Jawlensky and Marianne von Werefkin by combining artist
similarity with the shortest connecting path in the underlying knowledge graph. Both cases
demonstrate how the system can support the transition from an overview of the data to the
exploration of individual artists and relationships.
Case Study 1: Identifying an atypical participant in the Munich
Secession
The first case study focuses on the Verein Bildender Künstler Münchens “Secession”. The
Munich Secession is an interesting case because artists associated with its exhibitions did
not necessarily share the same relationship with the organization. While some were
members, others could have participated only as invited guests. Our domain expert used the
filtering and cluster exploration functions of the ArtVis Embedding Explorer to find whether
such differences were reflected in the embedding.
Examining the distribution of artists associated with the Munich Secession. She began
the analysis with an overview of the complete artist embedding. The view shows the clusters
calculated for the complete dataset as well as the artists classified as noise. We then select
the Verein Bildender Künstler Münchens “Secession” as a filter criterion. The resulting view
displays the existing global cluster assignments and highlights the artists that match the
selection.
The filtered artists are distributed across different clusters, showing that their contexts in the
underlying graph are not very similar. In one of the global clusters, only a single artist
matches the selected filter (see Fig. 1). This artist, named “Krabbé Hendrik Maarten”
appears untypical compared with the other artists displayed for the Munich Secession. This
observation does not mean that the artist forms an independent one-person cluster. Instead,
the artist is the only member of an existing global cluster that remains visible under the
selected criterion.
Investigating the artist’s participation. To understand this result, the user selected the
artist and inspected the information provided in the detail view. This artist participated in
many group exhibitions, including exhibitions associated with the Munich Secession.
However, the available group information does not indicate that the artist was a member of
the Munich Secession or of the other groups with which they exhibited. The combination of
repeated exhibition participation and the absence of membership suggests that the artist
may have participated as a guest rather than as a member.
This distinction offers a possible explanation for the artist’s unusual position within the
filtered result. The other displayed artists may be connected to the Munich Secession
through more regular or institutionally defined relationships, whereas this artist’s connection

appears to be based primarily on exhibition participation. The visualization shows attention
to a difference that would be difficult to recognise from a list of participating artists alone.
Returning to the complete embedding. Our domain expert then removed the filter and
inspected the artist’s position in the complete dataset (see Fig. 2). The artist belongs to a
cluster containing additional artists who appear to have participated in exhibitions organised
by different groups without necessarily being recorded as members of those groups. Our
domain expert interprets that cluster may capture a broader pattern of guest-like participation
rather than an association with one particular organisation.
The cluster assignment alone does not establish that these artists were invited guests.
Membership information can be incomplete, and similarity in the embedding can result from
several relationships represented in the knowledge graph. Nevertheless, the observation
generates a concrete research hypothesis: some artists may be grouped together because
their exhibition histories are characterised by participation across multiple organisations
without corresponding group memberships.
This case study shows how filtering and cluster exploration can support the identification of
atypical cases within an art-historical category. The system does not directly determine the
artist’s institutional status. Instead, the ArtVis Embedding Explorer reveals an unusual
distribution, provides access to the relevant exhibition and membership information, and
guides the researcher towards a distinction between formal membership and temporary
participation that warrants further investigation.
Figure 1: Filtered view of the artists associated with the Verein Bildender Künstler Münchens “Secession”. Hendrik Maarten
Krabbé is the only matching artist from Cluster 15 displayed after applying the filter.

Figure 2: Complete view of Cluster 15 after removing the filter. The selected artist, Hendrik Maarten Krabbé, is shown within the
context of all 101 artists assigned to the cluster. The group distribution inside the cluster is also displayed on the left side.
Case Study 2: Investigating the connection between Jawlensky and
Werefkin
The second case study focuses on the relationship between Alexej von Jawlensky and
Marianne von Werefkin. The two artists had a close personal and artistic relationship. They
moved to Munich in 1896 and later became associated with the artistic circle surrounding
Wassily Kandinsky. Their shared biography, therefore, provides an established art-historical
context against which the results of the ArtVis Embedding Explorer can be examined.
This case is particularly useful for demonstrating the relationship between two different
analytical functions. The artist comparison shows how similar the artists are within the
embedding, while the shortest connecting path identifies a concrete connection between
them in the underlying ArtVis graph.
Comparing the two artists. We begin by searching for Alexej von Jawlensky and selecting
him as the first artist in the Artist Comparison view. We then search for Marianne von
Werefkin and select her as the second artist. The system reports a comparatively high
similarity between their embeddings (see Fig. 3). This result is consistent with the existing
knowledge of their close personal and artistic relationship.
To examine a specific connection, we continue the analysis using the Shortest Connecting
Path view.
Tracing the connection through the exhibition network. The shortest-path view displays
the entities connecting Jawlensky and Werefkin in the underlying graph. Based on their
known activities after moving to Munich, one might initially expect the path to be primarily
associated with exhibitions, groups, or contacts in Germany. The path, however, includes the
Russian Salon of 1909 (see Fig. 4), revealing an additional connection within a Russian
exhibition context.

This observation extends the initial analysis beyond the artists well-known relationship in
Munich and Kandinsky’s circle. It directs attention to an exhibition that may have played a
role in both artists exhibition histories. For the user, the Russian Salon therefore represents
a less immediately expected point of connection and a possible starting point for further
research.
The shortest path should not be interpreted as confirmation that the Russian Salon caused
the high embedding similarity. Artist similarity and graph connectivity describe different
aspects of the data. The similarity value indicates that Jawlensky and Werefkin have
comparable contexts or shared relationships within the modelled data. The shortest path
identifies one concrete route connecting them, but it is not necessarily the only connection or
the most historically significant one.
Further investigation will be required to determine the importance of the Russian Salon
within its respective exhibition history. Relevant questions include whether both artists
participated in the same edition, how their works were presented, which other artists or
organisations were involved, and whether the exhibition contributed to a broader exchange
between Russian and German artistic networks.
This case study demonstrates how the ArtVis Embedding Explorer can combine
computational similarity with an interpretable network connection. The system first supports
the identification of a strong similarity between two historically connected artists and then
provides a concrete exhibition context through which this relationship can be investigated.
The ArtVis Embedding Explorer confirms the expected connection and also reveals a less
obvious international context for further art-historical research.
Figure 3: Artist comparison between Alexej von Jawlensky and Marianne von Werefkin. The embedding view shows the
positions of both artists and their similarity value of 0.715.

Figure 4: Shared graph context and shortest connecting path between Alexej von Jawlensky and Marianne von Werefkin. The
path connects both artists through the Salon 1909 exhibition.
